claim: Multicellular organisms orient their mitotic spindles relative to neighboring cells to form and maintain organized tissues.
source: To form and maintain organized tissues, multicellular organisms orient their mitotic spindles relative to neighboring cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general biological principle.

claim: A molecular complex scaffolded by the GK protein-interaction domain (GKPID) mediates spindle orientation in diverse animal taxa.
source: A molecular complex scaffolded by the GK protein-interaction domain (GKPID) mediates spindle orientation in diverse animal taxa by linking microtubule motor proteins to a marker protein on the cell cortex localized by external cues.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The GKPID complex links microtubule motor proteins to a cortical marker protein localized by external cues.
source: A molecular complex scaffolded by the GK protein-interaction domain (GKPID) mediates spindle orientation in diverse animal taxa by linking microtubule motor proteins to a marker protein on the cell cortex localized by external cues.
evidence: This mechanism is described in the abstract and detailed in the introduction with citations.

claim: A single historical substitution can recapitulate the evolution of GKPID's capacity to bind the cortical marker protein.
source: The complex was assembled through a series of molecular exploitation events, one of which – the evolution of GKPID's capacity to bind the cortical marker protein – can be recapitulated by reintroducing a single historical substitution into the reconstructed ancestral GKPID.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: The single historical substitution revealed and repurposed an ancient molecular surface that previously had a radically different function.
source: This change revealed and repurposed an ancient molecular surface that previously had a radically different function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis in Figure 7.

claim: Multicellularity evolved independently in several eukaryotic lineages using unique mechanisms each time.
source: Multicellularity – defined as the differentiation and spatial arrangement of cell types into functioning tissues within an integrated organism – evolved independently in several eukaryotic lineages, using unique mechanisms each time to drive the cellular functions necessary for tissue organization (Rokas, 2008; De Smet and Beeckman, 2011; Trillo and Nedelcu, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Many protein families involved in animal cell adhesion, signal transduction, and cell differentiation first appeared in the genomes of unicellular eukaryotes that were progenitors of animals.
source: Comparative analyses have established that many protein families involved in cell adhesion, signal transduction, and cell differentiation in modern animals first appeared in the genomes of unicellular eukaryotes that were progenitors of animals (King, 2003; Nichols et al., 2006; Richter and King, 2013; Rokas, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cells that orient the spindle parallel to the epithelial plane expand the tissue.
source: Cells that orient the spindle parallel to the epithelial plane, for example, expand the tissue; those that rotate it orthogonally to the plane escape the epithelium, as in epithelial-mesenchymal transitions during development (Morin and Bellaïche, 2011; Gillies and Cabernard, 2011; Nakajima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cells that rotate the spindle orthogonally to the epithelial plane escape the epithelium, as in epithelial-mesenchymal transitions during development.
source: Cells that orient the spindle parallel to the epithelial plane, for example, expand the tissue; those that rotate it orthogonally to the plane escape the epithelium, as in epithelial-mesenchymal transitions during development (Morin and Bellaïche, 2011; Gillies and Cabernard, 2011; Nakajima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The spindle orientation complex has been most extensively studied in Drosophila melanogaster neuroblasts.
source: The complex and its functions have been most extensively studied in Drosophila melanogaster neuroblasts, but it plays a similar role in birds and mammals (Saadaoui et al., 2014) and in other cell types, such as several kinds of epithelium (Nakajima et al., 2013; Saadaoui et al., 2014; Bergstralh et al., 2013; Bell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The spindle orientation complex plays a similar role in birds and mammals.
source: The complex and its functions have been most extensively studied in Drosophila melanogaster neuroblasts, but it plays a similar role in birds and mammals (Saadaoui et al., 2014) and in other cell types, such as several kinds of epithelium (Nakajima et al., 2013; Saadaoui et al., 2014; Bergstralh et al., 2013; Bell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In the spindle orientation complex, the scaffold is the GK protein interaction domain (GKPID) of the protein Discs large (Dlg).
source: In this complex, the scaffold is the GK protein interaction domain (GKPID) of the protein Discs large (Dlg), which binds microtubule-associated motor proteins, such as the kinesin-3 family member KHC-73, and the Partner of Inscuteable protein (Pins in insects, LGN in vertebrates).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: GKPID binds microtubule-associated motor proteins, such as the kinesin-3 family member KHC-73.
source: In this complex, the scaffold is the GK protein interaction domain (GKPID) of the protein Discs large (Dlg), which binds microtubule-associated motor proteins, such as the kinesin-3 family member KHC-73, and the Partner of Inscuteable protein (Pins in insects, LGN in vertebrates).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: GKPID binds the Partner of Inscuteable protein (Pins in insects, LGN in vertebrates).
source: In this complex, the scaffold is the GK protein interaction domain (GKPID) of the protein Discs large (Dlg), which binds microtubule-associated motor proteins, such as the kinesin-3 family member KHC-73, and the Partner of Inscuteable protein (Pins in insects, LGN in vertebrates).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Compromising Dlg's GKPID or other components of the Pins-Dlg-KHC-73 complex causes impaired spindle orientation, tumorigenesis, defects in cell polarity and differentiation, and developmental failures of tissue organization.
source: Indeed, compromising Dlg's GKPID or other components of the Pins-Dlg-KHC-73 complex affects numerous tissues and cell types by causing impaired spindle orientation, tumorigenesis plasia, defects in cell polarity and differentiation, and developmental failures of tissue organization (Nakajima et al., 2013; Johnston et al., 2009; Siegrist and Doe, 2005; Bergstralh et al., 2013; Yoshiura et al., 2012; Bilder, 2000; Woods, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The GKPID has been found only in animals, choanoflagellates, and Filasterea.
source: The GKPID has been found only in animals, choanoflagellates, and Filasterea (te Velthuis et al., 2007; de Mendoza et al., 2010), but it is similar in both sequence and structure to the guanylate kinase (gk) enzymes, which are common to all life and regulate nucleotide homeostasis by catalyzing the transfer of phosphate groups from ATP to GMP (Li et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: GKPID is similar in both sequence and structure to the guanylate kinase (gk) enzymes.
source: The GKPID has been found only in animals, choanoflagellates, and Filasterea (te Velthuis et al., 2007; de Mendoza et al., 2010), but it is similar in both sequence and structure to the guanylate kinase (gk) enzymes, which are common to all life and regulate nucleotide homeostasis by catalyzing the transfer of phosphate groups from ATP to GMP (Li et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Guanylate kinase enzymes are common to all life and regulate nucleotide homeostasis by catalyzing the transfer of phosphate groups from ATP to GMP.
source: The GKPID has been found only in animals, choanoflagellates, and Filasterea (te Velthuis et al., 2007; de Mendoza et al., 2010), but it is similar in both sequence and structure to the guanylate kinase (gk) enzymes, which are common to all life and regulate nucleotide homeostasis by catalyzing the transfer of phosphate groups from ATP to GMP (Li et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: gk enzymes were recovered from taxa across the tree of life, suggesting a universal distribution.
source: We recovered gk enzymes from taxa across the tree of life, suggesting a universal distribution, as previously reported (te Velthuis et al., 2007; de Mendoza et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: GKPIDs are present in all animal genomes analyzed as well as in their closest unicellular relatives, the choanoflagellates and Filasterea.
source: In contrast, GKPIDs are present in all animal genomes analyzed as well as in their closest unicellular relatives, the choanoflagellates and Filasterea; however, GKPIDs are absent from the genomes of all sequenced fungi and all other eukaryotic and prokaryotic lineages analyzed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: GKPIDs are absent from the genomes of all sequenced fungi and all other eukaryotic and prokaryotic lineages analyzed.
source: In contrast, GKPIDs are present in all animal genomes analyzed as well as in their closest unicellular relatives, the choanoflagellates and Filasterea; however, GKPIDs are absent from the genomes of all sequenced fungi and all other eukaryotic and prokaryotic lineages analyzed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: All GKPIDs cluster together as a monophyletic group, with the gk enzymes forming a paraphyletic set of basal lineages.
source: All GKPIDs cluster together as a monophyletic group, with the gk enzymes forming a paraphyletic set of basal lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The gene that came to code for GKPIDs was generated by duplication of an ancient gk enzyme before the last common ancestor of Filozoa and after the split of Filozoa from the lineage leading to fungi.
source: This topology indicates that the gene that came to code for GKPIDs was generated by duplication of an ancient gk enzyme before the last common ancestor of Filozoa (animals+choanoflagellates+Filasterea) and after the split of Filozoa from the lineage leading to fungi, which contain no GKPIDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic topology shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Anc-gkdup is an active guanylate kinase enzyme with a Michaelis constant (KM) comparable to that of the human enzyme.
source: We found that Anc-gkdup is an active guanylate kinase enzyme, with a Michaelis constant (KM) comparable to that of the human enzyme, albeit with a slower kcat (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Anc-gkdup displays no measurable Pins binding.
source: It displays no measurable Pins binding and failed to orient the mitotic spindle in living cells (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Anc-gkdup failed to orient the mitotic spindle in living cells.
source: It displays no measurable Pins binding and failed to orient the mitotic spindle in living cells (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Enzyme activity is the ancestral function of the gk/GKPID family.
source: These data indicate that enzyme activity is, as predicted, the ancestral function of the family; further, the scaffolding functions associated with spindle orientation were not yet present, even in suboptimal form, when duplication of the gk enzyme gene gave rise to the locus leading to GKPIDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental characterization of Anc-gkdup.

claim: The scaffolding functions associated with spindle orientation were not yet present when duplication of the gk enzyme gene gave rise to the locus leading to GKPIDs.
source: These data indicate that enzyme activity is, as predicted, the ancestral function of the family; further, the scaffolding functions associated with spindle orientation were not yet present, even in suboptimal form, when duplication of the gk enzyme gene gave rise to the locus leading to GKPIDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental characterization of Anc-gkdup.

claim: Anc-GK1PID has no detectable guanylate kinase activity.
source: Specifically, we found that Anc-GK1PID has no detectable guanylate kinase activity, but it binds Pins with moderate affinity and is highly effective in orienting the mitotic spindle in cell culture (Figure 2A,B,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Anc-GK1PID binds Pins with moderate affinity.
source: Specifically, we found that Anc-GK1PID has no detectable guanylate kinase activity, but it binds Pins with moderate affinity and is highly effective in orienting the mitotic spindle in cell culture (Figure 2A,B,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Anc-GK1PID is highly effective in orienting the mitotic spindle in cell culture.
source: Specifically, we found that Anc-GK1PID has no detectable guanylate kinase activity, but it binds Pins with moderate affinity and is highly effective in orienting the mitotic spindle in cell culture (Figure 2A,B,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Anc-GK2PID orients the mitotic spindle and binds Pins with even higher affinity than Anc-GK1PID.
source: We also reconstructed Anc-GK2PID – the more recent progenitor of all Dlg proteins in the ancestral animal – and found that it too orients the mitotic spindle and binds Pins with even higher affinity, suggesting a subsequent fine-tuning of Pins-binding capacity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The capacity of the GKPID to bind Pins and orient the mitotic spindle arose well before the evolution of animals or multicellularity itself.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that the capacity of the GKPID to bind Pins and orient the mitotic spindle arose well before the evolution of animals or multicellularity itself.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional characterization of ancestral proteins and their phylogenetic positions.

claim: The capacity of GKPIDs to carry out spindle orientation functions evolved before the evolution of organized multicellularity.
source: The capacity of GKPIDs to carry out these functions therefore evolved before the evolution of organized multicellularity itself, because filastereans do not form organized colonies (although cells from some species do aggregate [Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic timing and the biology of filastereans.

claim: KHC-73 orthologs are clearly present in animals, choanoflagellates, and Filasterea.
source: We found that KHC-73 orthologs are clearly present in animals, choanoflagellates, and Filasterea; fungal genomes do not contain a convincing ortholog of KHC-73 but do contain a closely related paralogous member of the kinesin-3 family (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence database searches and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The KHC-73 gene is as old as the Filozoan ancestor.
source: This observation indicates that the KHC-73 gene is as old as the Filozoan ancestor and originated during the same phylogenetic interval in which Anc-GK1PID evolved its novel functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the taxonomic distribution of KHC-73 orthologs.

claim: The genome of Salpingoeca rosetta contains an ortholog of Pins that is very similar in sequence and domain architecture to its metazoan orthologs.
source: The genome of Salpingoeca rosetta, a choanoflagellate that forms spatially organized spherical colonies (Dayel et al., 2011), contains an ortholog of Pins, which is very similar in sequence and domain architecture to its metazoan orthologs ( Figure 3 , Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis and shown in Figure 3.

claim: A Pins ortholog is present in Monosiga brevicollis.
source: A Pins ortholog is also present in another choanoflagellate, Monosiga brevicollis, but none was detected in Fungi, Filasterea, or any lineages outside of choanoflagellates and animals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence database searches.

claim: No Pins ortholog was detected in Fungi, Filasterea, or any lineages outside of choanoflagellates and animals.
source: A Pins ortholog is also present in another choanoflagellate, Monosiga brevicollis, but none was detected in Fungi, Filasterea, or any lineages outside of choanoflagellates and animals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence database searches.

claim: The GoLoco domain exists only in animals and choanoflagellates.
source: Indeed, a key domain of Pins – the GoLoco domain, a simple 23-amino acid sequence that mediates Pins' contact with membrane-associated G-proteins and is therefore crucial to its cortical localization (Smith and Prehoda, 2011) – exists only in animals and choanoflagellates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: Pins evolved before the split of choanoflagellates and animals.
source: This observation establishes that Pins evolved before the split of choanoflagellates and animals and suggests that it evolved after a functional GKPID emerged in the Filozoan stem lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the taxonomic distribution of Pins orthologs.

claim: Pins evolved after a functional GKPID emerged in the Filozoan stem lineage.
source: This observation establishes that Pins evolved before the split of choanoflagellates and animals and suggests that it evolved after a functional GKPID emerged in the Filozoan stem lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic timing of GKPID and Pins evolution.

claim: The association of GKPID with Pins in the spindle orientation complex evolved through a stepwise process of molecular exploitation.
source: The association of GKPID with Pins in the spindle orientation complex therefore evolved through a stepwise process of molecular exploitation (Bridgham, 2006) – a form of exaptation in which a newly evolved molecule recruits as a binding partner a more ancient molecule, which previously had different functions and a fortuitous but unrealized affinity for its new partner.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic timing and functional characterization of the components.

claim: S. rosetta GKPID binds the D. melanogaster Pins linker peptide with moderate affinity.
source: We found that S. rosetta GKPID binds the D. melanogaster Pins linker peptide with moderate affinity (Figure 4A), corroborating our finding that GKPID's capacity to bind metazoan Pins originated before the common ancestor of animals and choanoflagellates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: S. rosetta GKPID does not detectably bind the S. rosetta Pins linker.
source: In contrast, S. rosetta GKPID does not detectably bind the S. rosetta Pins linker: in a simple pull-down assay using a glutathione-S-transferase/Pins fusion protein and His-tagged GKPID, we detected no association of the two S. rosetta proteins under conditions in which the orthologous pair of proteins from D. melanongaster shows robust binding, even though both S. rosetta proteins are expressed and soluble (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Dividing S. rosetta cells appear to orient their mitotic spindles relative to the surface of the colony in a way that maintains the colony's spherical geometry.
source: We visualized the mitotic spindle in colonial S. rosetta using fluorescence microscopy and found that dividing S. rosetta cells appear to orient their mitotic spindles relative to the surface of the colony in a way that maintains the colony's spherical geometry (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Individual dividing S. rosetta cells that are not organized into colonies orient their spindles relative to the flagellum and the apical-basal axis.
source: We found that individual dividing S. rosetta cells that are not organized into colonies also orient their spindles relative to the flagellum and the A-B axis (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Spindle orientation in S. rosetta is likely to involve internal marks imposed by the cell's polarity rather than cues from neighboring cells.
source: Because spindle orientation relative to the cellular axis occurs in both colonial and noncolonial S. rosetta cells, spindle orientation is likely to involve internal marks imposed by the cell's polarity rather than cues from neighboring cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both colonial and non-colonial cells orient their spindles.

claim: Seventy-one amino acid replacements occurred along the phylogenetic branch between Anc-gkdup and Anc-GK1PID.
source: The potential candidate mutations are those that occurred during the phylogenetic interval between Anc-gkdup and Anc-GK1PID – the same branch on which the transition to GKPID function took place. Seventy-one amino acid replacements occurred along this branch, making identification of the functionally important changes an apparent challenge.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on ancestral sequence reconstruction.

claim: Substitution s36P virtually abolished the catalytic activity of Anc-gkdup and established moderate-affinity Pins binding.
source: Substitution s36P, located where the hinge meets the binding lobe, virtually abolished the catalytic activity of Anc-gkdup and established moderate-affinity Pins binding (Figure 6A,B; lower and upper case residue symbols denote ancestral and derived states, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Substitution s36P gave Anc-gkdup the capacity to robustly mediate spindle orientation in cultured cells.
source: In cultured cells, this single substitution also gave Anc-gkdup the capacity to robustly mediate spindle orientation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Substitution f33S conferred Pins binding and decreased but did not abolish enzyme activity.
source: Substitution f33S, also in the hinge, had largely similar effects, conferring Pins binding and decreasing – but not abolishing – enzyme activity; the affinity of Anc-gkdup+f33S is almost identical to that of AncGKdup+s36P, suggesting that f33S may also confer spindle orientation capacity, although this possibility was not directly tested.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Combining f33S with s36P did not further shift the protein's function beyond that caused by either change alone.
source: Combining f33S with s36P did not further shift the protein's function beyond that caused by either change alone (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The three substitutions in the binding interface (s34C, a73G and f75Y) caused minor reductions in enzyme activity but did not confer even moderate Pins-binding.
source: In contrast, the three substitutions in the binding interface (s34C, a73G and f75Y) caused minor reductions in enzyme activity but did not confer even moderate Pins-binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A single substitution – either s36P or f33S – was sufficient to recapitulate the evolution of the new functions that emerged during the evolution of the GKPID.
source: The genetic basis for the evolutionary origin of the GKPID's spindle-orienting functions therefore appears to have been very simple. A single substitution – either s36P or f33S – was sufficient to recapitulate the evolution of the new functions that emerged during the evolution of the GKPID and to completely or partially abolish the ancestral function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Residue 33 does not contact the ligand.
source: Residue 33 does not contact the ligand, and residue 36 makes only a minor and apparently nonspecific contact to Pins at one end of the binding site (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Residue 36 makes only a minor and apparently nonspecific contact to Pins at one end of the binding site.
source: Residue 33 does not contact the ligand, and residue 36 makes only a minor and apparently nonspecific contact to Pins at one end of the binding site (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The residues that compose the Pins-binding surface are almost entirely conserved from Anc-gkdup to Anc-GK1PID.
source: Overall, the residues that compose the Pins-binding surface are almost entirely conserved from Anc-gkdup to Anc-GK1PID (Figures 5B, 7A,B), and the backbone structure of the binding lobe is almost identical between the crystal structures of extant GKPIDs, gk apo-enzymes, and a gk apo-enzyme containing mutation S36P (Figure 7B, see also ref. Johnston, et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis shown in Figures 5B and 7A,B.

claim: The backbone structure of the binding lobe is almost identical between the crystal structures of extant GKPIDs, gk apo-enzymes, and a gk apo-enzyme containing mutation S36P.
source: Overall, the residues that compose the Pins-binding surface are almost entirely conserved from Anc-gkdup to Anc-GK1PID (Figures 5B, 7A,B), and the backbone structure of the binding lobe is almost identical between the crystal structures of extant GKPIDs, gk apo-enzymes, and a gk apo-enzyme containing mutation S36P (Figure 7B, see also ref. Johnston, et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Pins binding surface appears to have been present even before the interaction with Pins itself evolved.
source: Thus, the Pins binding surface appears to have been present, even before the interaction with Pins itself evolved.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural conservation of the binding surface.

claim: The key portion of the Pins-binding surface of GKPID was derived without significant modification from the ancient surface that gk enzymes use to bind GMP.
source: Homology models of the ancestral proteins, as well as the structures of extant family members, indicate that the key portion of the Pins-binding surface of GKPID was derived without significant modification from the ancient surface that gk enzymes use to bind GMP (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: GMP and Pins share a key structural feature: a negatively charged head flanked by a small hydrophobic region.
source: This GMP-binding site could be repurposed for binding Pins because the two ligands – one a nucleotide, the other a peptide -- share a key structural feature: a negatively charged head flanked by a small hydrophobic region (Figure 7A,B, ref. Johnston, et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The phosphate group at the head of GMP is anchored to the enzyme with hydrogen bonds to four clustered residues that form a positively charged pocket (R40, R43, Y80, Y82).
source: Specifically, the phosphate group at the head of GMP is anchored to the enzyme with hydrogen bonds to four clustered residues that form a positively charged pocket (R40, R43, Y80, Y82); in the GKPID, these same residues form hydrogen bonds to the phosphate group of Pins' phospho-serine 436.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: In the GKPID, residues R40, R43, Y80, Y82 form hydrogen bonds to the phosphate group of Pins' phospho-serine 436.
source: Specifically, the phosphate group at the head of GMP is anchored to the enzyme with hydrogen bonds to four clustered residues that form a positively charged pocket (R40, R43, Y80, Y82); in the GKPID, these same residues form hydrogen bonds to the phosphate group of Pins' phospho-serine 436.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: The historical hinge substitutions s36P or f33S inhibited enzyme activity and conferred the novel scaffolding function on GKPID by restricting the ancestral enzyme's dynamic hinge motions and/or changing its occupancy of conformations that have high affinity for Pins.
source: We therefore propose that the historical hinge substitutions s36P or f33S inhibited enzyme activity and conferred the novel scaffolding function on GKPID by restricting the ancestral enzyme's dynamic hinge motions and/or changing its occupancy of conformations that have high affinity for Pins.
evidence: This is proposed based on structural and functional analysis.

claim: The GKPID complex was assembled stepwise through a process of molecular exploitation.
source: Our work indicates that the GKPID complex was assembled stepwise through a process of molecular exploitation, in which old molecules with one function are recruited into a functional binding interaction with a newly evolved molecule.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the evolutionary analysis.

claim: The GKPID already had the fortuitous capacity to bind the Pins protein, even before the latter protein appeared.
source: In this case, the GKPID, a duplicate of an ancient enzyme with an essential metabolic role in all life forms, already had the fortuitous capacity to bind the Pins protein, even before the latter protein appeared or subsequently acquired its relatively simple GKPID-binding linker motif (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the evolutionary analysis and shown in Figure 8.
